author: reek
body: Arithmetic inside a proposition. A proposition is parsed by parse-type, and until this shipped the type grammar had no infix operators, so `1 + 1 === 2` stopped at the operator: the grammar returned the bare `1`, the claim parser read the `+` as the proof name, and the failure surfaced as CDX1000 on the token after it.

author: reek
body: The operator is an ordinary application spine now, which is the shape the proof normalizer already reduces, so each claim below is folded to a literal and checked by Refl rather than admitted on faith. The negative guard is codex/test/errors/prop-arith-false.

author: reek
body: The precedence claim is the one that can fail. A single left-associative loop reads `1 + 2 * 3` as `(1 + 2) * 3`, which is 9, so admitting 7 is what says the multiplicative level binds first.

author: reek
body: A negative literal is one atom, not a minus applied to something. Before that shipped, `parse-type-atom`'s catch-all took the bare `-` and left the digits behind, so `-2` could not sit on either side of a `===` and the normalizer had to refuse to fold any negative result -- folding one would have named a literal the grammar could not write.

author: reek
body: `sub-neg` is the claim that needs both halves at once: the left side folds to a negative and the right side has to parse as one.
